summary.text: The disproof specializes to \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and uses arbitrarily large primes: for a prime \(p\), the only admissible integers up to \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)=2\). Choosing \(p\) beyond both the asserted threshold and \(e^4\) gives \(\sqrt{\log p}>2=a(p)\), contradicting the proposed lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ divides }n\}.
\]
(As usual, the set of prime factors of \(1\) is empty, so \(1\) is always counted.) We disprove the assertion
\[
\forall \epsilon>0\;\exists N\;\forall n\ge N,
\qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n).
\]

The key observation is that
\[
a(p)=2
\]
for every prime \(p\).

Indeed, consider an integer \(k\) counted by \(a(p)\). Thus \(1\le k\le p\), and every prime factor of \(k\) is a prime factor of \(p\). Since \(p\) is prime, its only prime factor is \(p\). If \(k=1\), then \(k\) is counted because it has no prime factors. Suppose instead that \(k>1\). Every integer greater than \(1\) has a prime divisor, so choose a prime \(q\mid k\). By the defining condition on \(k\), this prime \(q\) must divide \(p\). Because \(p\) is prime, it follows that \(q=p\). Hence \(p\mid k\), and therefore \(p\le k\). On the other hand, \(k\le p\), so \(k=p\). Conversely, both \(1\) and \(p\) satisfy the required condition and lie between \(1\) and \(p\). Thus the only integers counted at the argument \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), proving \(a(p)=2\).

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the asserted eventual lower bound were true. Apply it with
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
There would then be an integer \(N\) such that for every integer \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1-1/2}=(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).
\]

Choose a prime \(p\) so large that
\[
p\ge N\qquad\text{and}\qquad p>e^4.
\]
Such a prime exists because primes are unbounded. For completeness, unboundedness follows from the standard Euclidean argument: given any bound \(B\), the integer \((B+1)!+1>1\) has a prime divisor \(p\); no prime at most \(B+1\) can divide it, since every such prime divides \((B+1)!\) and hence cannot also divide a number differing from that factorial by \(1\). Thus \(p>B+1>B\). Applying this with a bound at least both \(N\) and \(e^4\) gives the required prime.

Since the natural logarithm is strictly increasing on the positive real numbers and \(p>e^4\), we have
\[
\log p>\log(e^4)=4.
\]
Both sides are nonnegative, so taking square roots preserves the strict inequality. Consequently,
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}=\sqrt{\log p}>\sqrt4=2.
\]

On the other hand, \(p\ge N\), so the alleged lower bound applies to \(p\), and the calculation above that \(a(p)=2\) gives
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)=2.
\]
This contradicts \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\).

Therefore the proposed statement is false. In fact, the obstruction is the infinite subsequence of prime arguments: along every prime \(p\), the value is constantly \(a(p)=2\), whereas for any fixed \(\epsilon<1\), and in particular for \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\), the quantity \((\log p)^{1-\epsilon}\) tends without bound as the primes tend to infinity.
